---
title: "Methods"
---

## What these numbers are

Each prediction is the output of a model trained on species that already have IUCN
assessments, applied to species that do not. The methods come from published work,
principally IUCNN. We did not develop a new method.

## What a probability means

`prob_threatened` is the model's estimate that a species would fall into a threatened
category if it were formally assessed. It is not a probability of extinction, and it is
not a substitute for the criteria IUCN applies.

## Why several predictions per species

A species may be run through more than one model, and models are re run as data improve.
We keep results for every run is kept. The species page shows all of them rather than one.
We think that agreement between independent runs is information on its own.
Yet, the consensus figure is the median across runs. The spread is the standard deviation. 

## Training and evaluation

Models are trained on assessed species and evaluated with spatially blocked cross
validation rather than a random split. Species that occur near each other share climate,
sampling effort, and often conservation status, so a random split lets information pass
between training and test data and inflates the apparent accuracy.

Performance is reported separately for threatened and non threatened species.

## Versioning

Predictions are never edited in place. A new release adds new files and the previous
release stays available. The changelog records what moved.

## Limits worth knowing

Predictions rest on occurrence data, and occurrence data reflects where people have
looked as much as where species are. Poorly sampled regions and poorly collected taxa
carry more uncertainty than the probability alone suggests.

These estimates are meant to direct assessment effort and research attention.
